DETAILED ACTION
Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Status of Claims
The amendment filed 02/17/2022, is acknowledged and has been entered. Claims 1-4, 6-16 have been amended. Claims 17-18 have been cancelled. Claims 1-9, 13-16, and 21-24 are allowed, while Claims 10-12, 19, and 20 are rejected.
Priority
Acknowledgment is made of applicant’s claim for foreign priority under 35 U.S.C. 119 (a)-(d). The certified copy has been filed in parent Application No. PCT/RU2019/050257, filed on 12/24/2019. Receipt is acknowledged of certified copies of papers required by 37 CFR 1.55.
Information Disclosure Statement
The information disclosure statements (IDS) submitted on 08/25/2021, 01/16/2023, 05/01/2024, 05/02,2024 are in compliance with the provisions of 37 CFR 1.97.  Accordingly, the information disclosure statement is being considered by the examiner.
Abstract
Applicant is reminded of the proper language and format for an abstract of the disclosure.
The abstract should be in narrative form and generally limited to a single paragraph on a separate sheet within the range of 50 to 150 words in length. The abstract should describe the disclosure sufficiently to assist readers in deciding whether there is a need for consulting the full patent text for details.
The language should be clear and concise and should not repeat information given in the title. It should avoid using phrases which can be implied, such as, “The disclosure concerns,” “The disclosure defined by this invention,” “The disclosure describes,” etc.  In addition, the form and legal phraseology often used in patent claims, such as “means” and “said,” should be avoided.
The abstract of the disclosure is objected to because it contains legal phraseology (i.e., relates to a nucleic acid encoding said antibody; a method for preparing said antibody, and use of said antibody).  Correction is required.  See MPEP § 608.01(b).
Drawings
The drawings are objected to because of lack of appropriate labeling of panels and conditions in Figure 3 as well as mislabeling of the Y axis. Additionally, Figure 2 should stand alone and therefore needs to indicate which panel (left or right, please label as A, B) was treated with the MA-042 antibody at what concentration (1pg/ml or 1 ng/ml, respectively). In Figure 3 the Y axis is labeled as “% of dead TRBV9+ cells”, however the specification text reds “number of dead T lymphocytes as a function of MA-042 concentration…” Please clarify by correcting the text to indicate that the measurement is of the fraction of dead cells, not their absolute number).
Corrected drawing sheets in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121(d) are required in reply to the Office action to avoid abandonment of the application. Any amended replacement drawing sheet should include all of the figures appearing on the immediate prior version of the sheet, even if only one figure is being amended. The figure or figure number of an amended drawing should not be labeled as “amended.” If a drawing figure is to be canceled, the appropriate figure must be removed from the replacement sheet, and where necessary, the remaining figures must be renumbered and appropriate changes made to the brief description of the several views of the drawings for consistency. Additional replacement sheets may be necessary to show the renumbering of the remaining figures. Each drawing sheet submitted after the filing date of an application must be labeled in the top margin as either “Replacement Sheet” or “New Sheet” pursuant to 37 CFR 1.121(d). If the changes are not accepted by the examiner, the applicant will be notified and informed of any required corrective action in the next Office action. The objection to the drawings will not be held in abeyance.
Claim Objections
Claims 10, 12, 22, and 24 are objected to because of the following informalities: lack of required conjunction (“or”) between the group members listed for disease selection (“wherein said disease or disorder is selected from the group: ankylosing spondylitis, celiac disease, T cell leukemia, T cell lymphoma”).  Appropriate correction is required. Final text should read “wherein said disease or disorder is selected from the group: ankylosing spondylitis, celiac disease, T cell leukemia, T cell OR lymphoma”.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112a
The following is a quotation of the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112(a):
(a) IN GENERAL. — The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor or joint inventor of carrying out the invention.
The following is a quotation of the first paragraph of pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112:
The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out his invention.
Claims 10, 12, 19 and 20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), first paragraph, because the specification, while being enabling for the treatment of a disease or disorder mediated by TRBV9-bearing T lymphocytes, does not reasonably provide enablement for the prevention of a condition involving the TRBV9 family beta-chain region of the human T receptor.  The specification does not enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the invention commensurate in scope with these claims.
Claim 19 is drawn to the use of the pharmaceutical composition according to claim 9, which comprises an antibody (Ab) or antigen-binding fragment (Fab) thereof according to claim 1 in combination with one or more pharmaceutically acceptable excipients, in the prevention or treatment of a disease or disorder mediated by the TRBV9 family beta-chain region of the human T receptor.
Claim 20 is drawn to the use of the pharmaceutical composition according to claim 11 (comprising an Ab or Fab thereof according to claim 1 and at least in a therapeutically effective amount one other therapeutically active compound) in the prevention or treatment of a disease or disorder mediated by the human T cell receptor bearing the TRBV9 family beta-chain.
Claim 10 is drawn to the pharmaceutical composition presented in claim 19, which originates from claim 9 and defines the pharmaceutical composition as claim 1’s Ab or Fab in combination with one or more excipient, for the specific treatment or prevention of ankylosing spondylitis, celiac disease, T cell leukemia, or T cell lymphoma.
Claim 12 is drawn to the pharmaceutical composition of claim 20, which originates from claim 11 and defines a pharmaceutical composition comprising a combination of claim 1’s antibody or Ag-binding fragment and one other therapeutically active compound in a therapeutically effective amount, for the specific treatment or prevention of ankylosing spondylitis, celiac disease, T cell leukemia, or T cell lymphoma.
The specification does not disclose relevant examples for the assertions made in claims 10, 12, 19, or 20 in that, despite providing guidance towards treatment of disease, significant additional research is required in order to determine how effective the composition(s) in these claims might be used in the prevention of ankylosing spondylitis, celiac disease, T cell leukemia, or T cell lymphoma.
Due to the absence of working examples in the specification, a person having ordinary skill in the art would not be enabled in the use the pharmaceutical composition of either claim 9 or claim 11, as disclosed, to prevent a disease or disorder mediated by the TRBV9 family beta-chain T receptor broadly, or ankylosing spondylitis, celiac disease, T cell leukemia, or T cell lymphoma, more specifically. As such, while the specification provides guidance towards the treatment of one of the aforementioned diseases after onset, there is no disclosure of any evidence that the approach as proposed could be used to prevent any of the mentioned TRBV9-mediated conditions. Furthermore, based on the claim language in claim 20, it appears the applicant is suggesting that TRVB9-bearing T cells are the causative agent of the diseases presented in the group consisting of ankylosing spondylitis, celiac disease, T cell leukemia, T cell lymphoma. If this is the case, then the administration of the pharmaceutical composition described in claim 11, from which claim 20 originates, must prevent the aforementioned disorder. Therefore, the lack of existent working examples in the specifications and the significant amount of additional research, amounting to undue experimentation for one skilled in the art, that would be required to determine how effective the combination of the pharmaceutical compositions disclosed is not commensurate with the content or scope of the disclosure.
Factors to be considered in determining whether undue experimentation is required are summarized in Ex parte Forman 230, USPQ 546 (BPAI 1986). They include the nature of the invention, the state of the prior art, the relative skill of those in the art, the amount of direction or guidance disclosed in the specification, the presence or absence of working examples, the predictability or unpredictability of the art, the breadth of the claims, and the quantity of experimentation which would be required in order to practice the invention as claimed. In considering the language used in claims 19 and 20 regarding the use of the anti-TRVB9 Ab/Fab in question to treat and prevent disease in the disease models named herein, one must assess what is the state of the art for therapeutic approaches to the prevention and management of autoimmune and oncological disorders.
WO/1990/006758 and WO/1994/005801 disclose monoclonal antibodies against B-chain regions of the human T cell receptor variable domains, belonging to the TRBV5-3/TRBV8-1 and TRBV3-1 families, respectively, that may serve as diagnostic tools and therapeutic treatments for rheumatoid arthritis.  Furthermore, in a model of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), which is an experimental mouse model mimicking human multiple sclerosis (MS) disease, Zhao and colleagues teach that public TCRB chains can confer susceptibility to autoimmune disease – specifically that TCRβ1 supports recognition of the MOG peptide targeted by autoreactive T cells and that TCRβ2-6 are key players in mediating demyelinating CNS disease (Zhao et al, Sci Rep, 2016). Petersen and colleagues teach that at least two populations of autoreactive T cells that recognize and respond to the DQ8-glia-a1 peptide (found in 95%+ of CD patients) have biased clonotypic repertoires that are composed of TRBV9 chains (Petersen et al, J Immunol, 2015).
Currently, the only effective treatment for celiac disease is a gluten-free diet, which causes inferior quality of life and economic burden, does not always achieve remission, and the improvement of symptoms while on a gluten-free diet is not adequate for diagnosis (Kivelä et al, Nat Rev Gastronterol Hep, 2021 & Silvester et al, Am J Gastroenterol, 2021).  Kivelä and colleagues teach that new molecular insights into pathogenesis of celiac disease have provided targets for novel therapeutic strategies, including gluten sequestration, treatments to reduce the permeability of intestinal epithelial cells, and blockade of transglutaminase 2. Additionally, the state of the art supports the treatment of refractory celiac disease with pharmacological agents that include steroids such as budesonide or prednisone, and while a recent phase 2a trial of an anti-IL-15 antibody failed to reduce the size of the autoreactive T cell population in the intestinal epithelia, there were improvements in secondary endpoints, indicating that immunotherapeutic interventions should be investigated further (Cattasi et al, Lancet, 2022).
Boulos and colleagues teach that state of the art treatments of ankylosing spondylitis include a combination of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), disease modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), biphosphonates, and immunomodulating biologics (Boulos et al, Drugs, 2012). TNF blockers are considered an effective method of addressing both axial disease and include infliximab, etanercept, golimumab, certolizumab, and adalimumab, which can be given as monotherapy or in conjunction with methotrexate (Maksymowych, 2007, Thera Clin Risk Man, 3(6), 1125–1133 and Amaral de Avila Machado et al, Rheumatol Int, 2013 (33:2199-2213).  Yin et al teach that current strategies now focus on direct neutralization of soluble disease-mediating factors such as interleukin17 (IL-17) via humanized antibodies including secukinumab or ixekizumab, which have been shown to produce a significant decrease in clinical disease score (Yin, Y. et al, Arthritis Res Ther 22, 111, 2020). Furthermore, recent teachings instruct on the use of TRBV targeting monoclonal antibodies to eliminate autoaggressive T cells in AS including those against, CD8+ TRBV9-bearing cells (Komech et al, Rheumatology, 2018; Yang et al, Nature, 2022; Britanova et al, Nat Med, 2023).
Taken together, while the state of the art does teach approaches to treatments to improve disease burden and patient quality of life, it does not support any known processes or products that have been successfully evaluated for the prevention of celiac disease or ankylosing spondylitis or other autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or multiple sclerosis.
T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (T-ALL) is a type of non-Hodgkin disease that can be categorized as either a lymphoblastic lymphoma (LBL) or acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). Current state of the art for first line treatments include chemotherapy, including dexamethasone, asparaginase, intrathecal chemotherapy, and methotrexate, as taught by Raetz and Teachey (Am Soc Hematol Educ Prog, 2016). Select patients may also be eligible for chemotherapy plus hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HCT) and/or radiation. Importantly, the art teaches that therapeutic approaches to the elimination of blood T cell malignancies can include targeted elimination of transformed T cell clones via the depletion of these cells based on their TRBV expression. Specifically, Lucero and colleagues teach that in the case of large granular T cell leukemia circulating T cell pool is dominated by a single TRVB clonotype, in the instant case, VB13.3, which could be killed by the administration of therapeutic antibodies (Lucero et al, Clin Cancer Res, 2023).
Immunomodulatory therapies have become of greater interest as more is understood regarding the molecular underpinnings of the pathogenesis of T cell malignancies. Previous art teaches that particular TCR VBs within the T cell repertoire define certain T cell malignancies.  For example, leukemic cell lines including Jurkat cells and Molt-4 cells express VB8 and VB2, respectively and new strategies are being developed to target these monoclonal cells via CAR T cells (Li et al, Nat Comms, 2022). TRBV9 specifically has been documented on the surface of T cells in an experimental murine model of EBV-induced T cell lymphoma (Toyabe et al, Clin Exp Immunol, 2003). However, the state of the art does not teach any current strategies by which TRBV targeting can prevent the malignant transformation of T cells.
The art also teaches the importance of the recent discovery of mutations of NOTCH family members which may contribute to transformation and be targeted by immunotherapies and/or gamma-secretase inhibitors (Litzow & Ferrando, Blood, 2015). Additionally, while recent studies teach the use of adoptive cellular therapy in conjunction with “vaccines” for the treatment of cancer (Hammerich et al, 2019, Nat Med; Ghilardi et al, 2024, Nat Med) these strategies are only used after the diagnosis of transformed blood cells and therefore do not truly address issues of cancer prevention. Therefore, the current state of the art teaches that the development of an Ab/Fab-mediated or CAR-engineered approach to treating certain autoimmune and oncological disorders is predictable, it does not provide rationale for the use of this strategy in the prevention of disease.
In light of the state of the art and the aforementioned references, the specification fails to teach how a persona having ordinary skill in the art might make and use the broadly claimed invention without undue experimentation. Thus, claims 10, 12, 19 and 20 are rejected.
Allowable Subject Matter
The following is a statement of reasons for the indication of allowable subject matter:
Claims 1-9, 11, 13-16, and 21-24 are allowed. Toyabe and colleagues (Clin Exp Immunol, 2003, 135(1):92-97) disclose a TRBV9-binding antibody/antigen-binding fragment (Fab) as well as a nucleic acid encoding the aforementioned protein. Furthermore, this group describes an expression vector, a host cell for producing the Ab/Fab after incorporation of the nucleic acid-containing vector, a method for obtaining said host cell and finally, a method for producing an antibody or an antigen-binding fragment thereof. The authors report that the disclosed antibody/antigen-binding fragment is able to bind to TRBV9 expressed on PBMCs of EBV-infected individuals.
After examination, it is established that the inventions disclosed in independent claims 1, 4-9, 14, and 15 are distinct from those described by Toyabe et al in that the amino acid sequences of the variable domains of the HC and LC of the antibody/antigen-binding fragment in the Clin Exp Immunol publication differ from those reported here in as SEQ ID NO.: 16 and SEQ ID NO.: 18. As such the aforementioned claims and their dependents are novel as they describe a previously unreported ab/Fab with extensive humanization and the ability to bind to the TRBV9 chain of the human TCR with high affinity. As such, these proteins may be eligible for use in the treatment of oncological and autoimmune diseases defined by immunopathologies originating from TRBV9 beta-chain-bearing T cells and their use in this capacity is previously unknown in the art and does not qualify as obviously apparent to one having skill in the art.
Conclusion
